chapters.title: The problem is choosing what to learn next
beats: The problem is choosing a worthwhile next learning step when time is limited and career-planning assumptions can change.
Siti Rosli is our fictional operations coordinator. She brings spreadsheet reporting, supplier coordination and document processing.
For this demonstration, she has four learning hours a week.
Which strengths transfer? Which gaps deserve that time? And what would justify a different direction?

Existing strengths, gaps and a reason to reconsider form the three parts of Siti’s question.

chapters.title: Every match has a reason
beats: We select Financial data analyst, one direction for discussion. It ranks second in this captured steady-adoption result, with a match index of sixty point seven eight.
The explanation shows two of five required skills declared: spreadsheets and stakeholder communication.
The scoring weights begin with forty-five percent for declared required-skill coverage.
Thirty percent comes from transferable strengths.
Twenty-five percent comes from research and scenario context.
They contribute eighteen, thirty and twelve point seven eight index points here.
The match result is an index, not an employment probability. Missing skills are prompts for review, not proof of inability.
